analysis.one_liner: Makes price gouging on scarce lifesaving drugs a crime during declared shortages.
analysis.headline: The bill to criminalize price gouging on scarce lifesaving drugs was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2011-2012 drug shortage crisis, hospitals were paying enormous markups for scarce drugs used in surgery and cancer care. This bill would have let the President declare a six-month "market shortage" for a vital drug when supply could not meet demand. While a shortage was declared, it would be a federal crime, punishable by up to three years in prison and a $5 million fine, for anyone in the drug distribution chain to sell that drug at an unreasonably excessive price taking unfair advantage of the shortage. Hospitals and doctors themselves were exempt from the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need scarce drugs for cancer treatment, surgery, and other life-threatening conditions, plus the hospitals buying those drugs. When a drug becomes scarce and only a few sellers remain, prices can spike manyfold; the bill would have used criminal penalties and injunctions to keep those prices tied to normal costs and margins during the emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cancer and surgery patients, and hospitals

how_it_helps.text: The President could declare a market shortage for any vital drug — one used to prevent or treat a serious or life-threatening condition with no other available source — for six months, renewable if the shortage persists [S2][S3].

During a declared shortage, selling a vital drug at an unreasonably excessive price, with intent to take unfair advantage of the shortage, would be a federal offense subject to injunction and penalties of up to 3 years in prison, a $5 million fine, or both, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately [S3].

The ban would cover every wholesaler and distributor in the supply chain nationwide in the shortage area, but not hospitals or physicians, and the Attorney General would weigh factors like added costs, added risks, and price disparities with pre-shortage levels before finding a price unreasonably excessive [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug wholesalers, distributors, and manufacturers would bear the risk. Sellers who raise prices during a declared shortage would face criminal exposure even when higher prices are the normal economic signal that attracts new supply, and the vague "unreasonably excessive" standard would be interpreted by prosecutors rather than clear rules.

drawbacks.text: Criminalizing high prices during shortages could backfire: the promise of higher returns is a main incentive for manufacturers to produce scarce, often low-margin generic drugs and for new competitors to enter a shortage market, so the bill could deepen the very shortages it targets.

The bill leaves "unreasonably excessive" to be determined case by case by the Attorney General under broad factors, giving prosecutors wide discretion over drug pricing and legal uncertainty for sellers trying to decide how to price a scarce product [S3].

The price controls apply only while a shortage is declared, so sellers could legally steepen price increases just before a declaration or after termination — a gap an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing shortages of drugs with no substitutes, protection from emergency markups is a real benefit, and the bill's exemptions for hospitals and doctors and its cost-and-risk factors show some care in design. But the criminal-penalty approach is blunt: economists would argue that letting prices rise is what draws new manufacturing into a shortage, and vague standards plus prison time could chill supply exactly when it is needed. A narrower civil-penalty or transparency-focused bill might have captured most of the benefit with less risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in late September 2012, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2013 without any committee action or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Schumer introduced the bill on September 22, 2012, joined by Sens. Merkley and Blumenthal as its only cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action is recorded [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug wholesalers and distributors kept complete freedom to price scarce vital drugs as they wished, while hospitals and patients continued paying whatever the shortage market bore.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: These firms were the direct target: during a declared shortage, any wholesaler or distributor selling a vital drug at an unreasonably excessive price would face injunctions and penalties up to 3 years in prison and a $5 million fine per continuing day. Their ability to profit from emergency markups on scarce drugs is what the bill would have taken away.

Manufacturers of drugs in shortage would have faced criminal pricing exposure too, and the risk of prosecution for raising prices could have discouraged them from producing or expanding supply of low-margin, shortage-prone drugs — a genuine drawback for patients. The bill's cost-and-risk factors gave them some room to justify price increases.

Hospitals were both protected and favored: the bill exempts them entirely from the pricing ban, so they would have kept flexibility in procurement while wholesalers' emergency markups on the drugs they buy were curbed.
